summary: ApolloCare is a friendly, human-centered health companion designed for astronauts on long-duration space missions. Instead of confronting crew members with cold clinical charts or stressful medical jargon, it centers around an interactive, animated human figure that visually shows how their body is doing at a glance. Through calm breathing visuals, gentle colors, and simple self-care tips, astronauts can easily review their vital signs and daily habits. For emotional wellbeing, ApolloCare offers peaceful check-ins, guided breathing pauses, soothing ambient music, and built-in voice narration so they can interact effortlessly without screen fatigue. The purpose of ApolloCare is to reduce stress and protect both physical and mental health during deep-space isolation, giving astronauts a comforting, intuitive way to care for themselves in a calm and supportive environment.
details:
ApolloCare is a visual health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long-duration missions. Far from Earth, with communication delays and no doctor nearby, a crew member has to understand their own health without a medical background. ApolloCare turns their measurements into a clear picture and tells them what to do next.

The astronaut picks a crew profile, identified by face recognition, and reviews a clickable body map where every system has a traffic-light status. Each status comes with a shape and a word, so it never relies on color alone. They can enter physical vital signs by keyboard or with the camera, or complete an emotional check-in. For every indicator, the app explains why it matters in spaceflight, how to measure it, what to do at each level, and when to alert the crew medical officer or the flight surgeon. Trend charts compare each person against their own personal baseline, not a population average. Each result links to the source behind it.

The camera runs entirely in the browser. It estimates pulse (remote photoplethysmography), fatigue, eye closure, yawning and posture. Face descriptors never leave the device, and mission history is stored only with the user’s consent.

The knowledge base has 21 indicators, 18 evidence cards covering astronaut studies, and 33 sources. These include the NASA Human Research Program evidence reports and NASA OSDR datasets: LSDS-8 (metabolic panel), LSDS-64 (urine immune panel), GLDS-530 (RNA-seq) and the PLoS Biology radiation data (pbio.3000669). We cleaned these datasets and documented their quality problems, such as mis-assigned reference ranges and likely sample artifacts.

The benefit is earlier detection of change. In our demo, an astronaut feels fine while ApolloCare shows that her sleep has dropped and her reaction time is 20% above her baseline. It links the two findings to published ISS research and suggests what to do that day. The intended impact is to support crew autonomy on missions to the Moon and Mars. The same approach could also serve any isolated or remote setting where medical help is far away.

We built the backend in Python with FastAPI and SQLite, and the interface as an HTML/TypeScript web app. It supports several languages and dark mode. Computer vision runs client-side in the browser.

The project is creative in three ways. It uses a personal baseline instead of population ranges, because the NASA datasets cover only four crew members. The emotional check-in is deliberately never turned into a mission-level diagnosis or traffic light. And every color the app shows traces back to a cited threshold.

Honesty shaped our design. The mission history in the demo is simulated. The NASA data are pre- and post-flight values from four crew members, not in-orbit measurements. Only sleep, heart rate and temperature have sourced thresholds. For the remaining indicators the app shows the trend only, so nothing looks like a clinical limit. Health texts still need review by a health professional, and the camera pulse still needs validation against a pulse oximeter. AI-assisted code is declared in AI_USAGE.md.
